Adult Allegheny pearl dace (Margariscus margarita) collected from headwater streams in West Virginia exhibit a maximum recorded total length of 16 centimeters [Li = 16 centimeters], a value that represents the asymptotic body size for the species in this portion of its range. This ultimate length is considerably smaller than that of many other cyprinids occupying similar lotic habitats, likely reflecting the constraints of the cool, low-productivity environments this species prefers. Field surveys indicate that the total length at which these fish first achieve sexual maturity is 11.3 centimeters [Lp = 11.3 centimeters], a measurement derived from the more commonly reported standard length of 9.4 centimeters. Puberty in this species appears to be more closely tied to the attainment of a specific body size than to a strict chronological age, a pattern common among small-bodied northern freshwater fishes. The total length at puberty was estimated from a large series of specimens captured during the spring spawning season, with gonadal inspection confirming the onset of reproductive capability at this size threshold. Reaching 11.3 centimeters in total length typically requires at least one full growing season in most monitored populations.

Newly hatched prolarvae of the Allegheny pearl dace emerge from demersal eggs measuring approximately 1.33 millimeters in diameter, and the wet weight at birth has been calculated at 0.0012 grams [Wwb = 0.0012 grams], reflecting the modest endogenous yolk reserves available to the endotrophic larva. This minute mass places the species among the smaller-bodied members of the North American cyprinid fauna at the onset of exogenous feeding. Once the yolk-sac larva transitions to active feeding, growth proceeds rapidly during the first summer. The ultimate wet weight attained by fully grown adults has been recorded at 36.2 grams [Wwi = 36.2 grams], a value that scales predictably from the ultimate total length through a length-weight relationship derived from extensive field collections. This adult mass is relatively modest compared to sympatric minnow species such as the creek chub, underscoring the pearl dace's specialization for headwater refugia where food resources are seasonally limited. The relationship between body length and mass conforms closely to a cubic power function, with minimal seasonal variation observed among reproductively active adults.

Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at 18 °C [T = 18 °C], the maximum reproductive output of Allegheny pearl dace has been characterized through detailed observations of spawning behavior. Females typically deposit a single clutch of approximately 11 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 11 eggs per spawning event], and individual females are capable of producing roughly one clutch every single day [F_R_i = roughly one clutch every single day] during the peak of the breeding season. This high-frequency reproductive strategy yields a substantial daily fecundity, with an average of about 11 eggs produced per day across the spawning period. The temperature of 18 °C appears to be optimal for gamete production and spawning activity, as reproductive rates decline sharply when water temperatures fall below 15 °C or rise above 22 °C. This thermal dependence likely constrains the effective reproductive window in wild populations, particularly in the cool headwater streams where this species is most abundant. The reproductive physiology of captive females mirrors that observed in nature during years with favorable thermal regimes.

Longevity records for the Allegheny pearl dace indicate that the maximum lifespan under natural conditions is 4 years [am = 4 years], a relatively short duration for a small cyprinid inhabiting temperate streams at a temperature of 13 °C [T = 13 °C]. This lifespan was documented in a mark-recapture study conducted in a Pennsylvania watershed where water temperatures averaged approximately 13 °C [T = 13 °C] throughout the growing season. Individuals rarely survive beyond their fourth summer, with annual mortality rates increasing markedly after the second reproductive season. The cool thermal regime of 13 °C [T = 13 °C] appears to slow the metabolic aging process somewhat, as populations inhabiting slightly warmer waters (15 to 17 °C) exhibit maximum lifespans of only three years. Senescence in this species is characterized by a noticeable decline in body condition and reproductive output during the fourth year, followed by natural mortality during the subsequent winter. Detailed otolith analyses from archived specimens confirm that the oldest individuals are consistently those from the coldest, most stable headwater environments.

The reproductive ecology of Allegheny pearl dace is closely tied to the thermal profile of their natal streams. Under the cool conditions typical of their preferred habitat, where summer water temperatures rarely exceed 18 °C, the maximum daily egg production rate has been calculated as approximately 11 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 11 eggs per day]. The wet weight at birth of 0.0012 grams [Wwb = 0.0012 grams] is remarkably consistent across populations, suggesting strong stabilizing selection on larval size at hatching. Comparisons with other members of the genus Margariscus reveal that M. margarita exhibits a slower life history pace than its congener Margariscus nachtriebi, which attains a larger ultimate total length of 16 centimeters [Li = 16 centimeters] but does so at the cost of a shorter reproductive lifespan. The ultimate wet weight of 36.2 grams [Wwi = 36.2 grams] is reached only by the oldest and largest individuals in a population. Field observations confirm that the total length at puberty of 11.3 centimeters [Lp = 11.3 centimeters] is rarely exceeded before the second year of life. The species' maximum lifespan of 4 years [am = 4 years] represents a classic trade-off between early reproduction and somatic longevity at a temperature of 13 °C [T = 13 °C].
